NASHVILLE, TENN, Jan. 2S.-Chief
Justice John X. Shields. of the Ten
nessee supreme court, was elected
United States senator for the long term
on the first ballot this afternoon, de-
feating Charles T. Gates, Jr., attorney
general. The final vote was Shields.
50: Gates, 81


Politics in Tennessee has seldom
taken more unusual turn than that
which pitted Judge Shields and General
Gates as rivals for the senatorship. For
years, until within the past fortnight,
they have been bosom friends, POLITICAL
ly and otherwise.


For dozen years General Gates has
been law partner of Samuel G.
Shields, brother of the chief justice, the
firm being completed by r. E. l..
Mountcastle, Democratic national COM
mitteeman. Eleven years ago General
Gates led the fight that landed Judge
Shields on the supreme bench, and
Judge Shields, in turn. championed
General Gates candidacy before the su-
preme court for the attorney general
ship. Three years ago, when the pres
ent supreme court was elected, General
Gates actively directed the campaign
for the ticket headed by Judge Shields,
the latter then being made chief jus
tice and General Gates being reelected
to the attorney generalship.

is strong and lasting and royal never
shows a sign of weakening, because IT is

One may smile at the little maid who
loves her dolly, battered and worn to a
shadow of one-time glory; but, after all,
one should not smile. For she loves, not
the worn-out wreck that she sees, but
all that the dolly stands for. For in the
days when she rocked and sang that
"prettiest doll in the world to sleep,
! why, it just closed its eyes and softly
sang back again. And when she talked
to it, and dressed it over and over again,
it was sweetly responsive to all that she
said and all that she did.


So why shouldn't she go on loving II,
for it wasn't its red and white cheeks
that were dear, nor its pretty blue eyes,
nor its hair so charmingly curled-it was
just its little dollself. And that was left,
you know, when its splendor was all gone,
lost in the mishaps out on the heath.
Better Not Smile.
And one thinks she's better not smile
at all at the little maid and her abiding
love for her sweet little doll" rather
wish that the loyal little heart of her
may go on growing more loyal and true



in all this world of many true folk are


the ones who select their friends. and
those closer than friends, because Of the
self-under cover, and then go on finding
them lovable still when the physical self


has lost half, or more than half, of its
glory.


They are the ones who help form the
ties that outride the storm and stress of
time and last until the sure hand of death
cuts them asunder. For they are the
ones who look back of the lesser attrac-
tiOns to the things that stand for self,
and when the physical charms pass away
there is the self to go on attracting for
ever.


Yes, one likes to see the little maid
true to her dolly when its pretty cheeks
are only a memory, and one likes to see
grown men and women stand by when
there is nothing left but the half that
never dies.


And one believes that men and women
all over the world are glad and proud
indeed TO inspire that kind of affection.

QUEBEC, September 26.-Eight children

age, were burned to death early today as
they slept in their home on st. Francois
street Trudel, his wife, the Oldest son,
Antoine, and one daughter were the only
members of the family left alive. They
were badly burned, and Mrs. Trudel may
not survive.


The house was a three-story wooden
structure. The Trudels owned 1t, but
rented rooms to five other families. The
Trudel family lived on the top floor, and
their escape was cut off. The father and
mother dropped Antoine from a window.
and he was severely hurt by the fall. A
neighbor rescued a baby girl. Mrs. Tru-
del was carried out by firemen.


The children who lost their lives were
four daughters and four sons, the young
est two years old.

of endeavor after successive failures
until the prize sought for was gained,
and the unremitting pursuit, may be
worth all the sacrifices. The discovery

a beginning In fact, that achievement
counts for hut little in itself. other

Almost every expedition has brought

that will be followed may have much

BERLIN, April 10, 1918.


Crown Prince William and his wife,
Princess Cecelie, have broken boldly
away from Hohenzollern tradition and
have decided to build modern, up to-
date residence fitted with every modern
convenience and luxury. No longer will
they occupy antiquated. medieval palaces
without heat, without running hot and
cold water and adequate bathrooms lack
Ing proper ventilation and sewage dis
posal These old castles may be pic
turesque and surrounded with the tradi-
tons of the family, but they are far from
being comfortable places i'm which to live
and bring up children.


So the prince and the princess are en-
gagged in building a new home that shall
be a palace befitting their rank, but at
the same time provided with every apph-
ance for household sanitation and physi-
cal comfort that money can buy Fur
thermore, the furniture is being designed
and built in England.


A representative Of a London furniture
house has been here for several weeks,
and the crown princess has made repeat
ed visits to Berlin to discuss designs with
him. Though the princess has many SYM
pathizers In Germany in her dislike for
furniture oi GERMAN design, tne young
couple are risking not only a storm of
indignation from the German industry
when the fact becomes known, but per-
haps permanent unpopularity from their
future subjects


German royalty may not follow English
fashions with impunity. This was shown
during the life of the emperor's father,
his wife. 1.-The Englishwoman," daughter
of Queen Victoria and mother of Emperor
William, having been unpopular almost to
the extent of dimming the great popu-
larity of Emperor Friedrich.

the correct time.

was unable to recover it. During
those two years the watch was not
moved from the place where it first
lodged. Yesterday Mrs. Miller was
gathering wild flowers along the bank
of the stream when she noticed a
glittering object in the shallow
water. To her surprise she dis
covered the object was her husbands
watch.

more when she saw that the watch

That old question whether the poor
prefer to read stories about themselves
rather than about the rich has been re-
vived in England and discussed by Sc
rial writers. Some believe that most
readers, whether poor or rich, prefer
novels dealing with a class different
from their own, and some maintain
that the majority Of readers are more
interested in their own class. Nobody
knows. But something undoubtedly
depends upon the novelist himself.
Dickens had no difficulty in interest
ing everybody in the poor. Thackery
made the well-to-do and the rich in
teresting. So does Howells. So does
Mrs. Wharton. And innumerable 9TH
ers.


On the other hand, Jack London,
Kaufman, James Oppenheim. and pos
sibly two or three others have sketched
wonderful pictures of lowly and OBJ
scure lives. The great American
novel," which may have been written,
but is still awaiting publication, will
deal neither with the rich nor the
poor exclusively. nor with the middle
class, but with all sorts and conditions
of men. 1t will be a novel of democ-
racy-neither aristocratic nor proleta-
rian.

der 10 keep steerage way.

NEW YORK, Jan. a thrilling
story of how Duke Kahanamoku, the
Hawaiian world champion swimmer
and winner of aquatic honors at Stock
holm, saved his life but lost an index
finger, in a desperate battle under water
with giant eel, is related today in a
special Honolulu dispatch to the Herald


The battle occurred Saturday at the


Dukes" practice grounds near Homo
lulu. The expert swimmer killed the
eel. but not before the monster had
nipped off the foreiiinger o. his right
rand. The loss may impair his SWIM
ming powers permanently.


Cries from persons on shore warned
other swimmers that something was
wrong with the champion and they
looked about for him but Kahanamoku
had disappeared. Suddenly there was
frenzied churning of water over
spot where the depth was ten feet and
one leg of the swimmer was thrust
above the surface desperatel wig
wagging for help. Then the leg was
dragged beneath the water again and
the churning recommended.


Finally Kahanamoku shot to the sur
face, exhausted and then sank again.
Friends dived for him and rushed him
to shore where he was revived while
other swimmers captured the body of
the eel which the duke had choked to
death with his hands. The eel was the
largest ever seen in Hawaiian waters.

To the fact that, in the months be-
tween winter and summer, one part OF
the country may be experiencing warm
weather while another section not far
removed may still have winter temper
atures, Forecaster VonHerrmann, OF
the local bureau, ascribes the outburst
of tornado storms which have swept
the middle West and have caused tor
rental rainfalls and floods.


A sudden rise of temperature in q
particular locality, he said to-day, de-
velops a low pressure area, into the
center of which the wind rushes from
every point of the compass. If there is
sufficient difference in the temperature
of this locality and the surrounding
districts, the swirl of winds grows mag
ically into a destroying atmospheric
demon which sweeps over the country
with terrific force until, its energy
spent, the clouds loose their water upon
the earth


Tornado Came From Coast.
The tornado which leveled buildings
in Omaha and brought death and de-
struction to the city, later travelling
eastward and causing the nations
greatest tragedy, had it's beginning in


the state of Washington about MarU
JIG, according to VOnHerrmann. The
cyclonic conditions were developed in


the manner described, and moved


swiftly eastward over the Western


states, depolishing homes, public
| buildings and farm houses as they
went.


When the middle West was reached


the force was greatly spent, and just as
the surcharged clouds lowered above
the river valleys OF Ohio and Indiana,
| they burst and deluged the cities and
hamlets below.


Hit Atlanta From Texas.
The windstorm which passed over
Atlanta was caused in the same man
ner, VonHerruann said. This one had
| its origin in the lower part of the
/ Western United States, swept over the
| Gulf states, passed near Corpus Christi
| Texas, and then swerVed toward Allan
ia, but not with one-third the force that
| propelled the tornado that spent its
| vengeance upon the Ohio and Indiana
| cities.


Because of the heat Of summer
! these cyclones virtually never happen
| later in the year, for all of the country
usually is uniformly warm at the same
time, and there is no undue rising of
| the heated air at one particular point.

duty regulating traffic ashore. distinguish

horses about 800 feet out to sea and
rescued seven persons in a disabled motor

swamped by choppy sea. and two wom-
en- in the party, with children in their
arms. were screaming for help while the
throng OF promenaders ashore stood
helpless. But the two bluecoats, mount
ed on first-class steeds that were good
swimmers, did not hesitate for moment
They simply wheeled their charges. SPUR
red them down over the embankment
onto the beach and plunged into the
surf The tide was such that the horses
had not gone more then seventy-fiye feet
before they were "on their legs and had
to swim.

half submerged, while great crowd on
the beach cheered their efforts. Cody
and Mcdonald not only reached the craft
in time to rescue the women and children
but went back a second time and tOWed
in the boat with it's men occupants.


Some hysterical women wanted to hug
the policemen's horses, and the animals
seemed to derive dumb pleasure from
being patted and applauded. AS for Cody
and Mcdonald the hot sun soon dried
their trousers and they did not bother to
go off duNy until their day was over.

light, and the greater part OF the time

cande.

From the Atlantic.


As one glances over the pages of his
tory, one finds wars, 1t is true. which are
blots upon the records of man: but one
also finds wars without which the world
would have been SO incomparably the
poorer that we could never have done
without them. And one also perceives
to his astaonishment il he is practical
man." that the wars which have been
gigantic blunders and crimes have all
been wars for the attainment of practical
ends, like territory, markets, or
wealth, while the wars which the world
could not have done without have all
been wars for abstract pr r.nciples, for
beliefs. for religions. for mad dreams
and seemingly impossible hopes. The world
could well spare the conquests of Napo-
leon, because the wars were merely for
Napoleon; but the world could not spare
the martial conflicts surrounding and
realizing the French revolution. because
Ii was a war for those abstract and sensi-
bic absurdities, liberty. equality and
fraternity. We could we'll spare the
Mexican war which was a fight for ter
ritory. but we could not at all get along
without the civil war, which was a war
for man.

two prisoners, father and son, before the
commissioner at Oban. They were ac-
cused of having, in crocodile form, killed
two women while the latter were cross
ing the river. AS they refused to swear
their innocence on the dominant ju-ju of
the town, they were brought before the


white man." who naturally decided that
there was no case against them. The
deputation. however, had not finished with
the matter. On returning home another
ju-ju was invoked. with the result that
the sop confessed that both he and his
father were guilty, and that they had
killed and eaten seven other men and
women.


Strangely enough, people accused of this
uncanny power nearly always acknowl-
edge their guilt, even when fully aware
that such confession will probably cost
them their lives. Ava Ita, an old woman
OF Oban. was suspected of being "a snak..
soul. and of sending out her familia
every night to lick a wound on her hus
bands ankle while he slept, and so pre-
vent it from healing. The chiefs of tn

CINCINNATI, Ohio. Jan. 5.-Sleeet,
snow and hail almost paralyzed all
sorts Of traffic of the highways of the
central States today, causing
heavy damage to the business interests.
A cold wave at midnight turned a
drizzling rain into sleet and early to-
day caused great interference to tele-
graphic and telephone communication
between the northern cities.


Railroad trains came into terminals
several hours late, while interurban
electric lines were compelled to cease
operation along lines parralleling the
Ohio river for a hundred miles. Ohio
river packet lines shared In the heavy
delays and heavier freight traffic was
abandoned.


Reports today indicate that the storm
was one of the worst ever known
throughout West Virginia, Indiana,
Ohio. and northern Kentucky. United
States weather department reports to-
day state that indications are that con-
tInued precipitation is expected, mean
ing heavier losses to transportation
lines now seriously embarrassed.
headline:

Through Central States

CHICAGO. September 13.-The recent
squirt of Minneapolis and the slump of
Milwaukee have rendered the outcome of
the American Association race, which a
few weeks ago was generally conceded
to the latter club, a most doubtful prop
osition. The Millers have gradually cut
down the Brewers lead until today but
two games separate the teams. Both
teams felt the sting of defeat yester-
day. Milwaukee going down before CO.
lumbus and Louisville licking Minneap-
oils.


Minneapolis, however, made a Dig gain
on Milwaukee Thursday, when they
twice defeated Toledo. while Milwaukee
was held up by rain. The season has
three weeks to go, and the outcome of
the fight will depend upon the staying
qualities of the two teams. Columbus
and Louisville. too. have fighting
chances, but they will have to develop
phenomenal streaks to get any higher in
the race than they stand today.

Industrial depression is almost inevi-
tably the aftermath Of war. The with
drawal of men from productive labor to
serve in the ranks and the waste OF
money worse than burned up are always
felt. Even our little war with Spain
checked business, and not only England
but all Europe suffered when the Boer
war bills were paid. Italy wrested Trip
oil from Turkey at comparatively little
expense in lives and treasure, but the
disturbance of industries in northern
Italy, the most prosperous and progress
i've part Of the kingdom, has resulted in
so much misery that strikes and riots
have assumed dangerous proportions.
Agriculture was neglected during the
war, and the cost of living has risen,
while manufacturers find trade depressed
and claim to be unable to pay higher
wages though the demands Of the united
workers amount to only half cent an
hour of added pay. Europe will have to
pay for the Balkan war next, and this is
what makes money dear and depresses its
stock markets England and the United
States have wasted neither time nor
money in preparing for war in the last
year, and will profit accordingly, though
both will feel the effects Of dear money
for some time. The Bank of England
has held its discount rates on a high
basis for nearly ten months, a longer
period of dear money in that center than
has been experienced since the Crimean
war some sixty years ago.

buried beneath huge rocks.

ly to the wreck by the signalman at the
mouth of the tunnel, who saw the col
lapse and telegraphed at once to head
quarters. A hurricane accompanied by
snow hindered the work of the rescuers.


The earthquake shock was plainly felt
here.

companies of militia are still guarding
the flood district, conditions on the west
side are gradually becoming normal.

this morning by the finding Of two more
bodies. making a total Of seventy-three.


Streets are becoming cleared. refugees
are returning to their damaged homes,
work of repairing and building new
bridges is under way. telephones are
working in some sections and one lone
street car plies the flooded district. BY the
middle Of next week officials hope to


have the Broad street bridge, the main
artery between East and West Columbus,
In operation.


State troops today began a systematic
search of the flats and piles of debris,
some of which were washed several miles
below the city. The two additional
bodies were found in this territory today.
Although the city is fast regaining
normal conditions, relief stations are
still being filled nightly by refugees.

JOHANNESBURG, South Africa, July

fifty others in fight yesterday be-
tween the strikers and the troops, con-
tinued throughout the night.

smiths store and firing became gen
|eral. Squads of cavalry with drawn

quently charging and scattering groups

stroy the electric lamps the light from

Secretary Daniels will discontinue
the voluntary resignation from the
navy of officers who have not attained
command rank. Such designations
have become frequent, particularly in
the construction department. Two
naval constructors were enticed from
the service in 1912, and two have left
during the present year.


The list of those who have resigned
during the past ten years is a large
one, and though, generally speaking,
they have found very much more
lucrative employment in civil life,
examples are not wanting of former
naval officers being cast off by their
civilian employers when the reorgani-
zation of their establishments by these
trained service men had been effected.


What Secretary Daniels has in mind
is that the men, who have obtained
thorough technical and professional
training at the expense of the govern
ment, should remain in the service
until they have worked out their
cost" This they would not ordinarily
do in their lieutenant grades; hence
the prescription of resignation by Of
fcers under the rank of commander.

From the Council Bluffs Nonpareil.


When four wheeled carriages made
their appearance in Spain in the days
Of Ferdinand and Isabella it was con-
fdentIy predicted that they would bring
the country to ruin. So strong did this
conviction become that statute was
enacted prohibiting certain and divers
persons from recklessly spending their
hard-earned savings for carriages. II
was the judgment of the wise men OF
that time that people were likely to
spend their money foolishly for luxuries
and In this manner bring upon them
selves want for actual necessities unless
they were curbed by rigorous laws. To-
day we have the same problem in the
auto world. And the wise ones are seek
ing to devise ways and means of pre-
venting people from mortgaging their
homes for the purchase price of joy
wagon. Human nature seems to change
but little with passing centuries. Roose-
Welt said every reform has its "lunatic
fringe" So il seems every generation
has a similar fringe.

Paris. Dec. 27-Paris theatres have
combined in a campaign against late
corners after the performances have
begun. During the present season the
annoyance is greater than ever before,
almost interrupting the players.


Hitherto the public has been warned
by the crescendo ringing of electric
bells that the curtain is about to rise,
but this proved useless. The next plan
was to lock the doors as soon as the
performance began, not allowing any
entrances until the end Of the act, but
this resulted in such loud and violent
disputes and quarrels that the remedy
was worse than the disease.


The new measure now enforced is
simply TO turn out the lights in the
Hobbies just before the curtain rises,
thus compelling the lingering specta-
tors to enter the auditorium. This
plan, put in practice during the holi-
days. works fairly well.

LONDON. July 2o.-Mrs Emmaline
Pankhurst. the suffragette leader, again
has succeeded in outwitting the police.
1t was thought she had been arrested
last night, but it was another woman

Grated their prisoner.


At first the whole affair was consid-
cred a hoax, but it developed into an
apparently well laid scheme whereby

fat by another passage while her i'm
personator was Turing away the police.


Late last night a woman emerged

walked feebly and was assisted TO a,
taXicab. The detectives who had
guarded the building day and night
since Mrs. Pankhurst escaped after the
rioting at the Womens Political and
Social union July 10 Immediately con-
cluded that Mrs. Pankhurst was at
tempting to flee. They jumped into the
cab as it was driving off and ordered
the driver TO proceed to Scotland Yard.
Before they reached their destination
they lifted the veil and discovered that
their prisoner was an unknown woman.


Sim ultaneously so men and women,
including a number of stout navvies.
gathered at the entrance as the veiled
woman leaning heavily on her sup
porters, descended the steps Imme-
diately there was clash between the
police and the women. Two de-
tectives managed to cling to the cab.
Aftev the taxi had rounded the corner
the crowd scattered. Within half an
hour the detectives reappeared and
resumed their investment of the prem
Uses.


Meanwhile. however, the fat was un-
guarded and it began to dawn on the
police that probably they had been
hoodwinked. There were lights in the
Pankhurst fat again tonight and there
were detectives in the streets, but all
information was refused.


Many mail boxes in London and the
provincial cities were damaged last
night. it is believed. by suffragettes

From the Louisville Courier Journal.


Over in Floyd County, Ind. some of
the Ohio river bottom farmers have dis
covered that the flood was not an un-
mixed evil, since 1t has left ffve or six
inches Of sediment on their lands, which
will fertilize the ground for years.


This is compensation for the barns. the
fences. the pig pens, the chicken coops,
and other farm fixtures which have
been borne away on the bosom Of the
waters The Ohio River takes heavy
tools from the bottom lands at times.
but IL gives something in return


The lowlands on the Kentucky side Of
the river are constantly being enriched
by the floods. The river fertilizes these
lands more effectively than the work
could be done by human hands. II dis
tributes the sediment impartially. and
thousands of acres are recreated and
re-endowed with productive power with
every recurring inundation. When the
waters fall away and the ground dries
out. the bottom farmer stirs the soil
and plants his crops. The harvest richly
compensates him for his efforts.


During flood periods the dwellers in
the bottoms suffer losses and privations
and endure discomforts which, to the
residents of the highlands. would be in
tolerable. There are those who marvel
that people live in such places, but the
lowlanders are mostly tenant farmers,
and they get better returns from the
rich river bottom soil than would be
possible elsewhere with the same ex-
penditure of effort. The foods attend to
the fertilizing and the farmer does the
rest.


The principal bottom crop Is corn. This
staple cereal fiourishes to perfection In
the lowlands along the Ohio River, and
corn failures are unknown Some crops
are better than others but all Of them
are good. There is no richer land any
where. and II Is made so by the annual
deposits of the floods.

ed upon with horror by the people of

| dren had been the bane of her exist

Let's drown them, Floy," the moth

CHICAGO, February 15.-Robert Webb,
automobile bandit and slayer of Police
man Peter Hart, has been captured here.
The capture was made after revolver
battle and desperate hand-to-hand
struggle. in which the highwayman was
dubbed into submission by half dozen
policemen.


Webb apparently had been hiding near
his old haunts on the South Side since he
killed Hart when the policeman tried to
arrest him several weeks ago. Out Of
funds, he telephoned to woman friend
for money. An alert telephone central
operator caught the message and notified
the police.


Hoped to Leave City.


Webb told the woman to bring $500 to
certain street corner, SO he could leave
the city. A hundred officers were soon
scattered around the neighborhood, and
a few minutes before the appointed hour
Webb was seen walking toward the rem
devious.


Two detectives started after him. Webb
saw the officers and ran into a building
and out the back way. He was seen by
other police. and the waiting officers took
up the chase. Many shots were ex-
changed


Webb was overtaken at last by Police
man Patrick Courtney, and with the aid
of other officers the bandit was taken to



Accuses Another Me-.


Webb declared he was in ST. Louis
when Hart was killed. He accuses Michael
Casella, proprietor of the house where
Hart found Webb. with doing the shoot
ing. Capt. Patrick LAWN. who has been
searching for Webb ever since Hart was
killed, said that Webb had been in Mo-
bile, Ala, for ten days since the shoot
ing.


The bandit is regarded as one of the
most resourceful and dangerous GRIM
inals ever captured in Chicago.

teen years ago this morning, when many

tiremen had the flames under control
before the city companies arrived

made fast again, while an investigation
OF the cause of TIE fire was begun.

Los ANGELES, Jan 26.-The steamer
Mackinaw. which left San Pedro harbor
at o'clock tonight, is now tied to a
wharf in the inner harbor with hole
in her starboard bow. That the vessel
was saved is little short of miraculous


The steamer, commanded by Captain
Johnson, left the harbor in charge Of
Port Pilot Krog


After the pilot left her the navigators
evidently lost their bearings in the
heavy fog which prevailed and ran into
the breakwater, stoving a hole into the
bow. Engines were stopped and the
helpless vessel drifted out to sea.


Lifeboats were sent to take off the
crew and passengers, and when the last
were rescued the vessel was three miles
out and in great danger of sinking.


Thirty-one persons were taken from
the distressed vessel, including Robert
Dollar and his daughter, Mrs. Grace
Dollar Dickson.


The tugs Listo and Scandal were sent
out to aid the vessel, and after con-
siderable effort the steamer was towed
into the still waters of the inner har-
Dor, where repairs will be made before
the journey can be completed.

crowd pressed forward and back be-

lone policeman beneath the potoffice
portico did was to yawn and look at

authorities in keeping the police re-
serves out Of sight. Had crisis arisen

but no crisis came, and the man in blue
under the postoffice clock remained the

Salonica, July 4.-The battle Of Kill
kish which has been in progress for
several days, ended at 10 o'clock this
morning in the complete route OF the
Bulgarians. The Tulgarians evacuated
the town IN disorder. abanCoring sixty
field guns and quick frers. Kilkish is
now in flames. The Greeks continue
their advance.


The battle for the possession OF Kill
kish continued throughout Thursday
The Greek right wing drove the Bull
garians into the mountains beyond
Likovan. while the centre made a Wig
orous frontal attack on Kilkish, with
which the bulgars still retained con-
tact. The Fourteenth Bulgarian di-
vision. under command OF General
Dimitrieff, was stationed here.


Toward midnight the Bulgarians
made a violent surprise attack with
strong forces, which the Greeks re-
PEELED. The Fourth Greek division
made an impetuous counter attack
and occupied the dominating height

eastward Of Kilkish.


Firing ceased at o'clock on Friday
morning, but was resumed two hours
later, when a violent Greek cannonade
prepared the way for a decisive as
sault. The big siege guns which gave
such wonderful results at Yanina. were
employed against the Kilkish batteries,
while attacking parties made flank
movement.


These operations proved successful
and Kilkish was occupied. Seventeen
Bulgarian siege guns were captured
The Bulgarians fed in the direction OF
Demirhissar fearing that their retreat
might be cut off by the Greek right
wing, which has advanced northward

help came.

the ground with the first volley. The in
iured were carried away by their COM
pa MONS. score of others were injured
by stones and missiles.

two of the strikers. Just when it seemed
that the police and detectives, who were
outnumbered almost ten to one, would
have to give up the fight, Sheriff Doyle
and fifteen deputies. armed with riot
guns, arrived. The Strikers awed by the
death-dealing, powerful guns and the
augmented forces. quickly dispersed.

wood. she got in trouble in successive
gales, and her master and crew were
forced to abandon her. Later she was
picked up by the revenue cutter Onon-
daga and towed into Cape Lookout cove.

ing made ready to resume her voyage.
Her crew returned to her and under her

taken into Hampton roads and from there

British West Indies, and her owners are
the Observation-Disclosures Steamship

NEW YORK, Oct. 22-Gov. Martin II.
Glynn today made the formal order for
a grand jury investigation in New York
county of Harry X. Thaw's escape from
Matteawan. on August II, and Attorney
General Carmody reappointed w. 7.
Jerome a special deputy attorney gen.
eral to conduct the probe.


Justice Gavegan. in the supreme
court today. swore in the grand jury,
and District Attorney Whitman said he
would sidetrack all routine cases until
the Thaw escape is threShed out The
inquisitoIs will begin hearing witnesses
tomorrow.


The investigation was ordered in
New York because of the contention of
the Dutchess county authorities that
the plot to free Thaw was Matched
here. The conspirators are said to have
formed their plans in West Side
saloon.


About forty witnesses have been sub
poenaed. including Howard Barnum
the guard whom Thaw pushed aside
when he ran through the asylum gate;
Mrs. James Maher, who saw the get
away from a window: Dr. Keib, med
ical Superintendent of Matteawan:

wagon that cloaked the approach of the
taxicab that carried Thaw down the
road until he jumped into the touring
car: and William Gordon, proprietor of
the hotel at Beacon. where Richard
Butler and the alleged conspirators
stayed while perfecting their plans.

The attitude OF the United State.
Supreme Court toward the liberal and
progressive legislation enacted by the
States during the past twenty years or
more is effectively shown by Boston
lawyer, whose compilation of decisions
has recently been printed as a public
document by the Senate.


The records show that between 1887
and 1911 the Supreme Court rendered
500 decisions in cases involving social
and economic laws. In only three in
stances were adverse judgments given.
One was the ten-hour labor law in
New York; another declared invalid
an Illinois antitrust law, which dis
eliminated against certain classes, and
the third very properly overruled the
Louisiana law which deprived citizens
of that State of the right to order in
surance by mail


The Supreme Court has upheld every
State labor statute brought before it,
with the single exception OF the New
York labor law; i; has upheld every
State antitrust law. with the single
exception of the Illinois instance: it
has sustained every law regulating
sales of pure food and other merchan-
disc and restricting conduct of mercan-
tile business; il has upheld every
State gambling. bucket-shop, and anti
grain option law; every State liquor,
prohibition license, local option, and
anti-cigarette law; every statute regu-
lating the cattle industry and cattle
diseases; every law, except the Louis
lana insurance law, regulating the con-
duct of business for the general well
fare; every law regulating railroad
rates and the management of rail-
roads; every law fixing or regulating
rates for public service corporations !;
every State banking regulation statute
every law regulating the business and
methods of insurance and telegraph
companies, and every law authorizing
public undertakings. 1t has uniformly
held that such Improvements, even If
interfering with private property, were
within the police power of the State.
Equal liberality has been shown in
dealing with cases involving all phases
of taxation.


This is a remarkable showing and
proves the assertion that the United
States Supreme Court, instead of being
reactionary, has been steady and con-
sistent in unfolding all State 1egisla-
ton of progressive type. If all the
courts in the land were imbued with
the same spirit there would be no agi-
tation for the recall of judicial de-
cisions.

springtime. a playlet in two parts, was
presented yesterday afternoon at the May
festival of the pupils of the Friends
School in shaded nook of the Friends

The story of the playlet hinges upon
the awakening of the Goddess Spring
from her long sleep, induced by the South
Wind The awakened goddess falls in
love with the brave youth, Damoetas,
whom she finds sleeping in glade.


The North Wind, angered at her early
appearance, pursues her with the snow
flakes. She has only time, as she fees

while she leaves her buds blighted on
the ground. But the East Wind, with

beams, come to the succor of the poor

mistress for her birthday celebration.

bids him sit beside her to watch their
sports and revels. In these the Dryads

One of the quaint customs OF the
world which is disappearing with one
OF the worlds queerest people Is the
snake dance Of the Moki Indians, who
live in sunny Arizona. This Ameri-
can state as most people know, needs
water--needs II more than anything
else--and the Moki snake dance Is a
religious ceremony, an invocation for
rain which shall keep the springs
alive and which shall induce the
thirsty desert sands TO give bounteous
:. crops OF corn, melons and beans.


The ceremony Is very long, taking
all day TO perform. Towards the
close Of the day the pagan priesthood
takes charge in view OF all the gath
cred tribe This is when the snakes
arrive. They have been captured
DAYS before and now lie on the
ground near the priests. all deadly
rattlers.


Each priest must grasp snake
and whites who have witnessed the
dance say that they take them in
their arms. seize them by the back

chanting and dancing about.


Finally the snakes are all thrown

mentary pause. then all the dancers
plunge forward. attempting to fill

In two or three seconds all the

eyes. binding her.

about to drop. The crowd below knew
something had happened and there

wipe the oil from her eyes with her
gloves. but only further obstructed
her sight.


FAINTS WHEN SHE LANDS

got instant control of the machine she
would be killed. She 'volplaned, al
though having no idea of her direction.
Soon she heard shout from one of the
spectators. After maneuvering slowly,
and aided by shouts from the field she
landed.


It was some time before she could
see after her eyes had been washed
out She retained her nerve until after
leaving the aeroplane. Then she
tainted and was carried to the Garden
City hotel where city physicians at
tended her.


REALIZES HER DANGER


II knew when the oil cup exploded" !"
said Miss Miller, that was in great
danger but also knew there was
only one way to save myself and that
was to free myself of all fear AL
though I couldn't see felt sure / was
going to come through the experience
safely"

SAYS she is the youngest woman to
take up flying as profession. She

There were many women on the field
and they cheered heartily when Miss
Miller landed safely.

NEW YORK. Jan. 6.--Every vessel
along the middle Atlantic coast was no
titled by wireless today to search for the
United States naval supply ship Panther
carrying a crew of twelve officers and
men, which has not been heard of since
she was caught by the full fury of Fri
days hurricane off Cape May.


For three days the shore stations from
New Jersey to the Carolinas have been
trying to get in touch with the Panther
by wireless, but no answer was received
TO any Of the queries.


Whether the Panthers wireless ceased
working and other wireless masts were
crippled or whether the disaster overlook
the ship has not been learned.


It was expected that if no word was re-
ceived from the ship soon the navy de-
partment would order warships to steam
out from Hampton Roads in search of the
Panther. The Panther left this port with
naval supplies for the United States sta
ton at Guantanamo, Cuba.


The supply ship was in communication
with land when the storm overlook her
and her wireless operator said she was
still standing the storm strain well. Then
communication was suddenly broken off.

A definite step toward a more moral
Wall street was taken the other day
when the New York Stock Exchange
appointed a committee to consider meas
ures to protect the investing public.

tute more desirable apparel for the
ragged habiliments that have ceased to
cover the streets nakedness Wall street
has been losing a great deal of business

has suffered much from the New Haven
and Frisco exposures. Such indecencies
have caused many investors to fee hor-
rified. Now there are numerous offices
to let in lower Manhattan where once
were to be found prosperous brokers
and their busy clerks. Reform in the
New York Stock Exchange has been
due for long time. The desire for
blue sky laws that has spread from one
state to another and the general indis-

bait have indicated that investors are

journey

Captain Clark once more struck the
right moment to send the two swim
mers away

Wright, and this fact gave her a big
battle against the ebb tide when she
reached the Marin shore.

tain Clark little after II o'clock yes

kept together until the buoy off Fort
point was reached. From this point
on Mrs. Wright showed better speed

condition.

have been able TO make her goal. The
hour and a half in the water had its

SAN FRANCISCO, January 1.-THE
centuries-old styles in clothing for both
men and women of China have come un-
der the disarproval of the cabinet of the
republic, and an edict has been issued
calling upon the women to abandon their
trousers for the occidental skirt and the
men to give up their comfortable loose
clothes for the sack business and con-
ventional evening clothes of the eau
casian.


A copy of the edict has been received
by Young Yew, consul here for the Chi
nese republic, together with pictures of
clothing prescribed for both sexes. The
vernacular papers here printed the edict
and illustrations yesterday.


The business derby and the formal silk
hat are the only two mentioned for men.
Nothing is said Of headgear for the wom-
en-, who, aside from hair ornaments, never
have worn head coverings.


Shoe Styles Prescribed.


Men are allowed high calfskin and low
tan shoes. while the women are limited to
high shoes to suit their taste.


Besides shoes, only three articles OF
dress are prescribed for women. One, a
loose-fitting garment on the lines of a
kimono is for house wear. An extremely
conventional pleated skirt and shirt waist
evidently are supposed to complete heI
wardrobe.


At the expressed wish of President
Yuan Shi Kai the edict, which was re-
ceived several days ago, was held until
New Year for publication.

According to the best obtainable sta
tistics, says Popular Mechanics, at least
1000 persons In New York spend their
entire working hours under ground.
These figures include the $500 employees
on the two subway systems now in op-
GRAFTON in that city. They also include
the 1000 men employed digging the new
subways and 100 men working several
hundred feet below the earth's surface
driving the aqueduct which is TO carry
through the Island Of Manhattan and
over into Long Island the waters that
are being brought down from the Catskill
Mountains.


Then there are more than 1000 men
and women who are employed In more
private enterprises that take them con-
stantly below the street surface. On quite
ordinary days l,5ooO 900 persons are ac-"n-
modated in New York subways and the
crowds are multiplying week by week.


In the great hotels OF New York the
mechanical departments are all far be-
meath the street surface. These kitchens.
bake shops. furnace rooms, engine rooms,
and laundries ordinarily are the cleanest
in the entire hotel.


Many OF New York's greatest depart
ment stores are connected directly with
the subways, as are also some Of its
newer theaters.


Last February a family of three from
San Francisco. visiting in New York,
lived for a fortnight in one of the most
fashionable and expensive hotels In the
city, spent most of their time shopping,
sightseeing, and theater-going, and only
once during the entire fourteen days
passed into the open air of the outside
world. From their rooms in the hotel
they were dropped by elevator to the
level OF the subway. Through the SUBJ
way they went to department stores,
theaters. and restaurants.


When they started for home they went
by subway from their hotel to the Grand
Central Station, and did not get out into
the sunlight until their train had well
started on its long journey. And this
was not on a bet. either.

To the fact that. in the months be-
tween winter and summer, one part OF
the country may be experiencing warm
weather while another section not far
removed may still have winter temper
atures, Forecaster NonHerrmann, OF
the local bureau, ascribes the outburst
OF tornado storms which have swept
the middle West and have caused tor
rental rainfals and floods.


A sudden rise Of temperature in a
particular locality, he said to-day, de-
velops a low pressure area, into the
center of which the wind rushes from
every point of the compass. If there is
sufficient difference in the temperature
of this locality and the surrounding
districts, the swirl of winds grows mag
ically into n destroying atmospheric
demon which sweeps over the country
with terrific force until, its energy
spent. the clouds loose their water upon
the earth.


Tornado Came From Coast.


The tornado which leveled buildings
in Omaha and brought death and de-
struction to the city, later travelling
eastward and causing the nations
greatest tragedy. had its beginning in
the state of Washington about March
16, according to VonHerrmann. The
cyclonic conditions were developed in
the manner described. and moved
swiftly eastward over the Western
states, demolishing homes, public
buildings and farm houses as they
went.


When the middle West was reached,
the force was greatly spent, and just as
the surcharged clouds lowered above
the river valleys of Ohio and Indiana
they burst and deluged the cities and
hamlets below.


Hit Atlanta From Texas.


The windstorm which passed over
Atlanta was caused in the same man
ner, NonHerrDann said. This one had
its origin i'm the lower part of the
Western United States, swept over the
Gulf states, passed near Corpus Christi
Texas, and then swerved toward Allan
ia, but not with one-third the force that
propelled the tornado that spent its
vengeance upon the Ohio and Indiana
cities.


Because of the heat of summer
these cyclones virtually never happen
later in the year, for all of the country
usually Is uniformly warm at the same
time. and there is no undue rising Of
the heated air at one particular point

lican organization. and also by Democrats.

ious partisanship. Many churches all
over the city received returns by special
wire and telephone. Protestants were for
Armstrong and Catholics for Porter. Both
are Protestant. but Mayor Magee, a

In Munich. the CAPITAL of Bavaria and
the most renowned art center OF Ger
many. unique geological garden has OF

The animals in this geological garden

conditions of their natural state. the
visitor thus being under the impression
that he sees the animals in their free
dom. This park for wild animals will b.
a practical combination of technical skill
and artistic beauty.


To the south of the city, where the pure
and fresh air blows. laden with the per
fume Of the great forests which cover
the hills and dales Of the Bayarian Alps.
and on the banks OF the river Isar, which
rushes down from the mountains. there
may be found the most beautiful land
scape in the environs Of Munich. Pine
trees hundreds of years old. together with
silver birches and knotty willows and
popars. form a forest I'm which small
lakes and brooks flow among thick bushes
and beyond far-stretching green meadows
rises a mighty mountain terrace. at the
foot of which are clear bubbling springs
This charming spot was chosen for
the laying out of geological garden ten
years ago when its present managing





the preliminary work.


A few years later the well known arch
itect Prof. Emanuel Won Sedl, took over
the artistic management and the archi-
tectural part of the gardens. The park
has been opened to the public for the
last two years.


Features of Gardens.


Coming to an open space in the woods
there are the mighty buffaloes. the former
inhabitants of the American prairies and
ancient forests. which the march of civ
ilization has almost extermnated. So
we find during our walks through the
magnificent park all kinds OF animals
the stays from the mountains OF Asia and
the wild boar from the forests of Europe
and India.


In the close vicinity of the buffaloes
from America are kept the European
bison from the swamps OF Russia-the
zebra and antelope from India, while
swimming birds from all part OF the
world sport on the lakes and streams.
There are white and black swans. peli-
cans and gulls and many other kinds of
fancy water fowl.

Miss Nan Secor, the seventeen year

South Highland avenue, Ossining, was
drowned in the Hudson River late
yesterday afternoon. Her father,
mother and two younger brothers were
helpless witnesses OF her death. Up
to a late hour last night the body had
not been recovered


Just before noon Mr.. and Mrs. Secor,
Miss Secor and Andrew and Frederick
Secor. aged ten and twelve years. had
started off for fishing trip. Loaded
with picnic baskets. they went to the
Shattemuc Yacht Club. and went on
board their power yacht, the Peggy.
The craft was brought 10 Ossining this
spring. and is well known for its
graceful lines and unusual speed for a
boat OF its type.


After fishing along the river for sew
eral hours the party started homeward
The motors were running at top speed.
Aided by stiff breeze, the Peggy was
slipping through the water at a fast
pace. The two little boys were sitting
with their mother in the bow OF the
boat.


Mr. Secor was at the steering wheel
near the stern. and Miss Secor was
leaning on the rail at his side. She
had forgotten that there was an open
ing less than foot from where she
was resting her arm. As the yacht
rounded Croton Point. the swells from
a passing steamer made the Peggy
rock Miss Secor lost her balance. She
grasped for the rail, but the next in
stant she had plunged into the river.


Almost as she struck the water her
father pulled the cord TO signal for
reversed motor Then he leaped into
the tender, trailing astern. and pulled
for the spot where his daughter had
disappeared. She rose once, struggling
weakly. but, before her father could
reach her, she had gone down again.


The yacht club was less than three
fourths OF a mile away, and soon a
dozen yachts and rowboats were
circlng around the spot where the girl
had disappeared. Several strong
swimmers dived again and again, but
could not find her. The tide was run
ming swiftly. and at last the searchers
were forced TO abandon their attempts.

sining National Bank and a member

& Co., at No. so Broadway. New York.

VERA CRUZ. Nov. 6.-The unrest
here today caused Admiral Fletcher to
deny shore leave to all officers and
men of the American warship fiotilla.
He wishes to avoid friction with the
natives. who are wildly excited over the
story that John Lind. President Will
sons special envoy to Mexico, had con-
firmed the reported notification that
General Huerta must relinquish the
provisional presidency.


Lind was silent today, but 1t was said
on good authority that he did not con-
firm the report that President Wilson
sent Huerta an ultimatum. Lind was
quoted as saying that the United States
had verbally told General Huerta that
he must resign and see to it that he is
not succeeded by any of his family or
close advisers.


This. of course, was nothing new, but
its repetition caused excitement among
the natives and the newspapers here


The United States now has seven war
craft here, and the report that two NOR
vessels have been ordered into Mexican
waters, made a decided impression on
the Mexicans. Admiral Fletcher has
made the Rhode Island his flagship in
stead of the Louisiana.


The German warship Bremen today
anchored of Tampico. Her commander
sailed from here after a conference with
Admiral Fletcher. and ii was reported
that trouble had broken out at Tampico,
but this was unconfirmed.

LEXINGTON, Va, Jan. 27.-The relay
squad of the White and Blue track
team has started active training for the
rapidly approaching track season.


The beginning of the indoor track
meeting is only three weeks of, and
hence a large number of men are re-
porting on Wilson field every after
noon. The mild weather is enabling
them to do outdoor work instead of
being confined to the gymnasium, as
has been the case heretofore.

team are exceedingly bright despite the
fact that Anderton and Groover, men,
bers of last seasons team, are not in
college. Hayne, Peoples and Glass have
been members of previous White and
Blue teams, and with them as a
nucleus, fast combination should be
developed. Glass was practically the
winner OF Washington and Lees VIC
tory over Richmond College last year.
At the South Atlantic intercollegiate
meeting at Baltimore last year he set a
new record for the quarter mile, going
the distance i'm 81 l-3 seconds. He is
the holder of the university record for
new men the most prominent are Dill
insham, Tarleton, Waggoner. Engle-
bert. and Harrison.


Tarleton won his track monogram at
Monson Academy, in Massachusetts,,
being one of the mainstays of the team
on the short runs and dashes Wag-
goner from Texas, has had consider
able experience on the cinder track at
TerrilI School in his home State Har-
rison. who has had training at Rich
mond Academy, and Wade, who comes
from the Texarkana High School, both
should win places in track athletics.


The weight men of last years track

sity record for the hammer throw,
while Peck has the record for the shot
put Yonan, record holder for the
broad jump, again will represent Wash
ington and Lee. and Thorn will run in

Christmas is the great holiday along

Vessels in Holiday Attire.

4 o'clock yesterday afternoon. News OF
the attack was not received until today,
communication having been cut by the
Iebels. The fighting lasted until night
faIL The federal losses were sixty killed
and about fifty wounded, while the rebel
losses are placed at twenty killed. The
rebels advanced in two columns from the
vest and northwest, driving the federals
back to the center Of the city. The fed
Grad gunboats were unable to take any
part in the fighting because of their posi-
hon. --.-. -


Dispatches received at the war office
Indicate that another attack was ex-
pected today, but up to a late hour no
news had been received.

at Tampico have transmitted to Vera
Cruz wireless requests for re-enforce-
ments. The cruiser Chester and the
British flagship Suffolk are en- route from

call The refugees who had gone ashore
from the warships after the rebel re-
pulse a few days ago again have sought
refuge aboard the warships.

been guarding the National Palace, was
sent to the suburbs today TO aid the
troops now engaged in the attempt to
drive back the Zapatistas. who have for
the last week been gradually closing in
on the capital.

Thousands of aliens who have declared
their intention Of becoming citizens of
the United States may be debarred from
realizing their hopes unless they file final
applications for naturalization papers be-
fore September 27. Richard X. Camp
bell. commissioner of naturalization, has
sent letters to all chief examiners
throughout the country. calling their at
tentfon to this situation.


Records show that there are 10000
aliens who have declared their intention
but have not filed final applications. A
large percentage of these made their
declarations before the enactment of the
present naturalization law, September
81, 1906. which requires that final APP
plications be made not less than two
or more than seven years after the
declaration of intention. Judge Jacob
Trieber of the Arkansas federal court
recently held that those who made
declarations under the old law and failed
to make final applications within seven
years after the passage Of the new act
would be barred from citizenship for
ever


Those who declared their intention
under the new law will have to wait
two years if they do not put in their
final applications before September 81.

reached. the troubles were just begin
ming.

fifty at the outside. Relief mad reached

towns partly or wholly wiped out. 1t

life will not reach more than fifty.

Relief work was going on with help
from Connersville and surrounding vii
lagos, and the situation was decidedly
encouraging. In Indianapolis a per-
feet organization cared for 1900 refu-
gees in public buildings, which had
room for more, and boats well pro-
visioned secured the area in West In
dianapolis and Broad Ripple, visiting
the last marooned household, which re-
fused to desert its property.

ands from their homes in all parts OF

drove the refugees unprotected to The

conditions Of life are resumed. In In
dianapolis. for example, three city
bridges, two interurban bridges. and
two railroad bridges were wrecked
The destruction of the West Wash
ington street and the Meridian street
bridges will interrupt for months
traffic with the west and the north
section of the city.


The rumors of great loss of life in
west Indianapolis have not been veri-
fed. and the death tolls will not be
more than ten. the police say. Water.
street car, and gas service were past

As the sun broke through fringe

The vote was 244 to 50, and when

Clark there burst forth a great volume

leries Joined.

Portland Me, Nov. 5-The death OF the
cook and the probable loss Of their cap
tain, Vincent Nelson, and three Of their
mates form part of a tale of the sea
brought here tonight by the survivors OF
the crew Of the Gloucester fishing schoon-
er Annie NJ. Parker.


The fact that their abandonment of the
stranded schooner near Nantucket and
the loss of life were unnecessary was not
known TO the crew until word reached
them tonight that the schooner was in
port at New Bedford, practically UNI
damaged.


Nine survivors of the Parker's crew
reached here aboard the lumber schooner
Triton, from Jacksonville. which had
picked them up from dories thirty miles
off Nantucket Sunday morning, after
they had been afoat twenty-four hours
without food or drink


Reuben Kenney. the cook, was swept
overheard from a dory while his mates
looked on, poweress to help.


The Annie VI. Parker, bound home from
the fishing grounds, went aground on
Rose and Crown Shoal, off the Nantucket
coast, early Saturday morning. The YES
sci was wracked by the waves, and the
crew agreed with Captain Nelson that
hope for safety lay in getting clear Of
their craft. So they abandoned her.


Three boats were put over the leeward
side before one was launched. The first
was smashed, and the second was
swamped, but the third was flcated and
eight men put out in it. Two other boats
were dropped overheard safely on the
windward side. The first held three men:
the last contained Captain Nelson and
three Of his crew.


II was pitch dark, and the dory crews
were lost to the view Of each other al
most in a moment The last seen of the
boat in which Captain Nelson left his
ship was when it was rounding the bow
of the schooner.


The men Of the other tow boats did
not see each other until daybreak When
they got together it was found that
neither had water or food.


They drifted about all that day and the
following night, constantly buffeted by
heavy seas, one of which carried Reuben
Kenney, the cook, over the stern. Ken
ney fought hard TO swim back TO the
boat, but went down before his comrades
could reach him.


When they were picked up by the Triton
on Sunday morning all the survivors were
nearly exhausted. The supplies aboard
the Triton were low and the ten added
hungry mouths taxed the schooners sup
ply TO the utmost. The Boston fisherman
Josie and Phoebe was sighted and hailed.
The skipper had no fish on board but he
set a trawl. lie pulled in a goodly catch
which, with flour and meal, was turned
over to the Tifton's captain.


Harry Nelson remained with the Josie
and Phoebe. in the hope that he might be
able TO obtain some trace of his father
and three mates.


BY an odd chance the Annie NJ. Parker
preceded her crew into a port. Staunch
and firm apparently, with only jib miss
ing, she was towed into New Bedford
to-day. raising the questions: why
should good ship be abandoned by her
crew." and Where was the crew."


The Parker had floated herself from
the ledge and had been sighted on Mon
day, drifting with all sails set, by the
British steamer Astrakhan. The steamer
placed a prize crew aboard and the
schooner arrived at the whaling port in
tow of the revenue cutter Gresham,
which was summoned by wireless.


The Parker sailed from Sydney, n. s.,
for Gloucester on October 26. Shortly
after leaving Sydney the fisherman ran
into northwest gales. With the run of
the tides she was driven far off her
course. After days Of jockeying with the
elements Captain Nelson found himself
on last Saturday morning near Nan
tucket, and was unable to work his vessel
off the lee shore.

hardship The waters of creek broke
through the mine wall and caught five
men. Two were washed by the rushing
water. to place of safety. but the
others were caught and imprisoned. After
many hours of labor the rescuers de-
SPARED of saving the men until faint tap
ping was heard. Then the rescuers, work.
ing in relays, redoubled their vigor, and

From the London Standard.


Near Lorrach. in the Black Forest. is
the strangest lake in the world It Is
called the Eichener See. and is perfectly
dry for from ten to thirteen years at
time, after which periods subterranean
springs refill the lake without any pre-
vious warning. flooding and destroying
any crops that have been planted.


The soil in the bed of the lake is very
productive, but the farmers and peasants
never know in what year their work will
be useless and their young crops
drowned" A few weeks ago the Eich-
ener See, after having been dry for ten
years. began refilling with water, which
in the deepest part is now fifteen feet,
the average depth being twelve feet. The
waters of the lake generally remain a
year or so, and then gradually dis
appear into the earth, leaving . rich
soil behind.

NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 27.-Cotton
was climbing to new altitude records
to-day until just at the close, when
a rumor, entirely uncorroborated, came
from Washington to the effect that
Oscar Underwood had introduced a
radical bill aimed against futures
trading.


On this rumor the ring went crazy
Pandemonium broke loose and every
man tried to sell his neighbor. There
was no support, and in the few min
utes before the gong October broke
from 1898 to 1854. The other active
months followed


New York had just closed for the
week when the news came. The panic
reigned only for the few minutes be-
fore the New Orleans gong.


According to the rumor, Under
woods bill is more radical than any
thing Senator Clarke proposed, and
Clarke's bill would have wiped out the
Cotton Exchange.

Special Cable to The Washington Herald.


London, Aug. 16.-Suits shot with gold
and cloths made OF blended colors are
amongst the new fashions for men for
next fall.


West End tailors say the most popular
suit will be of blue cloth shot with gray
and gold. London society men seem to
be demanding more variety and dainty
materials in their wearing apparel now.


Sackville Street tailors are preparing
for big rush for these blended blue
suitings.


Overcoats, too, are being revolutionized.
The new fashion is blue, shaped to the
waist, single-breasted and buttoned
through with only two buttons.


Silk hats are becoming more popular.
New models have shorter crowns and
hatter set brims. The reason for the
increasing popularity is that the crown
is only five and. three-quarter inches high,
and is less "bell-topped."


These hats have been selling at the
rate of fifty day by one Bond Street
dealer for weeks.

CAMP PERRY. Ohio. August 2s.-Ths
first fatal accident to happen on the
Ohio ranges at Camp Perry occurred
today, when Francisco Zegarra Ballon
Of the Peruvian team was killed by one
Of his fellow-countrymen, Juan b. Ze.
CARA, who accidentally pulled the
trigger Of his loaded rife.


Francisco Zegarra Ballon had gone
to his tent to rest when Zegarra. who
had just returned from the 800-yard
range, knelt in the street near his
tent and took aim with his rife at the
pole of Balloons tent just across the
way. Believing his gun unloaded. he
pulled the trigger. The resulting dis
charge sent bullet clear through the
tent pole and Ballon's left side. Bal
Ion succumbed Immediately.


Zegarra is frantic over the accident.
Ballon was a native Of AreQuipa,
Peru.

Bear traders again took charge Of the

ness.

expected that the current level would at
tract enough buying to sustain the mar

the market.

response to weekend covering. Losses
were made up and eventually many stocks

days close.

Pronounced heaviness developed this
week in several prominent stocks includ
ing New Haven New York Central,
Pennsylvania and American Telephone.

lowest prices for years.


Heaviness of these and other stocks were
resisted by the general market for a
time. but gradually the list as a whole
moved off.


Passing of the New Hoven dividend not

but upset the general market. Poor
railroad earnings, contracting business
and tight money reacted unfavorably on
stocks.

inhabitants of Dunnville and other set
Elements along the Grand River re-
turned to their homes today when the
great flood that began Saturday was
seen to be subsiding. The main streets
and many of the houses in the lower
section of the city are still well under
water and the property damage is
heavy. No deaths have been reported.


The flood was caused by the sudden
forming of an ice-jam behind Long
Bridge just below here. The water
backed UP rapidly and soon poured
over the embankment along the west
end of Dunnville. At Guilph and
Brantford the flood reached high
water mark.


Many families were forced to vacate
their homes and take refuge with those
living in the u'gher sections. All the
churches were closed yesterday.

MANCHESTER, ENGLAND, March
24.-While the independent labor party
was holding its convention here today
a number of suffragettes stole up and
placed padlocks upon the doors of the
hall When the delegates attempted to
leave, they found the doors locked on
the outside One enraged delegate
climbed out on the roof and paid his
compliments to the suffragette move
ment in picturesque language. Anoth-
er delegate smashed a window and tried
to crawl through, but he got stuck in
the aperture and hung head downward
for nearly 20 minutes, meanwhile
screaming and kicking violently.


The suffragettes had placed chains
across the doors, and hammers and
chisels had to be brought into play
before the doors could be opened.
Meanwhile the hungry delegates were
clamoring in the assembly room. One
man, who prOfessed sympathy for
the feminist movement, was set upon
by his companions and roundly beaten.
As soon as they were released from the
assembly room, they selected the big
gest and stoutest delegates to act as
guards about the building during the
balance of the session

But for the wireless telegraph, summoning. aid
from all directions until halfscore of vessels were
gathered about her. the Volturnos disaster would
suredly have been vastly costly in life than it
was. The fact that all the rescuing ships sent out
their leboas and that of them failed to gather
in some members of the Volturno's company, makes
clear that the loss would have been much greater if it
had mot been possible to draw together such flock
of rescuers.


There are lessons in this affair of the Volturno
only less impressive than those of the Titanic. The
Titanic, an "unsinkable' ship, went down by the
head in incredibly short space after her collision
The weather was clear and the sea CLASSY smooth


The Volturno was lost under very different cond-
tions. A terrific gale blowing, lifeboats could
not be launched, the sea was fearfuly rough. For
many hours, with impoent rescuers gathered around
them, the crew and passengers of the fated ship
fought the fire, and apparently their own magnificent
fight responsible for saving their lives. The gale
at last went down.. and then for the first time
factor in coping with great maritime disaster, the
experiment of pouring oil on the troubled waters
undertaken with complete success. The Standard
Oil tank ship Narragansett was among those that had
answered the distress signal Her captain, doubtless
after conference by wireless with the other COM
manders gathered about, undertook the task Of oil
ing the seas; pumping out the contents of his great
tanks while his vessel made a complete circuit of
the burning steamer. 1t is declared that this had
immediate effect in smoothing the waters, so that
lifeboats could live, and the work of carrying away
the survivors of the Volturno was taken up.


The heroism that marked the Titanic tragedy ap-
pears to have characterized this latest horror of the
sea- Men of three or four nations, in vessels flying
as many flags appeared in the company of eager res
cuers, and all did everything that was possible in tine
circumstances.

Among the Hopi the women are far
from occupying a servile or subordinate
position. The women own the houses,
the wife receives the newly married
husband into her home: the children
belong TO her clan and receive her clan
name. She is considered the owner Of
all household goods food supplies and
other possessions of the family. The
men perform all outside and field labor.

10 the live stock and see that the wants

vided for


In civilized communities this would
all be considered matter OF course,
but among the American Indians 1t is
nowhere paralleled. This is by no
means all that is expected Of the Hopi
husbands.


They must shear the sheep, card the
wool and weave blankets. belts, cere-
monial robes. and evening dresses and
shawls for the women. On occasion
they must even mind the babies and
help with the housework. Strangely
enough, the women build the houses,
although the men must cut the timbers
on distant mesas, transport them to the
villages on the backs of mules or burros
and place them in position as ordered
BY the builders.-The Christian Herald

New York. March 25.-With her mind
hopelessly unbalanced by the horrors
of an East Indian famine. Miss Mar
garet Reynolds, Il Presbyterian mis-
siona-y, twenty years old. returned to-
day on the steamship Verona, on her
way to Waterloo, Iowa.
On the pier to meet her stood Walter
H. Thompson, OF Chicago. her be-
-rothed. He had been told that the
only hope of restoring the girls mind
was the possibility that she might
recognize him.


Many passengers knew that this cru
cial test was to occur, and clustered
near when the young man rushed up
the Gangplank and along the deck
Reaching out his arms to her he called
her name.


The girl slowly turned her head and
stared at him blankly. He called again.
No answering look came into her eyes
She shrank back


By this time most Of the women had
turned away. weeping. The man was
led away sobbing.


Miss Reynolds was in Lahore during
famine. and for months. working day
and night to relieve the suffering, saw
sights of extreme horror.


Within three months the girl was a
wreck. and the only hope physicians
held out was that familiar surround
ings and friendly faces might restore
her reason.

MOBILE, Ala, January 10.-Results
of the search for victims of yesterdays
boiler explosion on the Tombigbee river
steamer James T. Staples indicated the
death toll would be larger than was
developed last night. Seven persons
were known to have been killed. OF
the eleven missing it is believed all are
dead.


Ten persons seriously injured will be
brought here today. All of the steam
er's chief officers were killed. About
half the victims are negroes. The
cause of the explosion has not been
definitely fixed.


The explosion occurred while the boat
was tied up at Bladon Springs, Ala.


The known dead are: Capt. Tom Bar
tee. Mobile; Coot Mckee. second clerk,
Mobile; Johnny Kopf. second engineer.
Mobile; Henry Moulton, mate, Mobile.


Five white persons and eleven negroes
were seriously injured.


After the explosion the boat sank up
to the cabin and then turned over on it's
side.

Mrs. Grace Macy Keefer. prom
inent society woman, probably will
take an appeal to the higher courts
from the decision OF Judge Bell denv-
ing her suit against David H Keefar
for alimony.


The decision came Saturday. fol-
lowing sensational testimony from
Mrs. Keefer, her son, Jack Macy and
from her divorced husband.


Mrs. KeefeF was frank, and her
frankness probably was the biggest
factor in the defeat of her own sui,
To questions by her husbands Law
yers she replied that she swears At
times, smokes cigarettes at times and
drinks at times.


Swearing is commonplace" shs
said, frankly. Nearly everybody does
it."


However. she said she did not
swear at her husband except when
he started swearing at her. She said
that sometimes he called her vile
names.


Her husband, on the stand later
denied some of his alleged actions
but admitted that he had slapped Mrs
Keefer after she called him a dirty
turkey buzzard,' because, She
charged, he had listened to her con
versation over the telephone.


Mrs. Keefer said she formed the
cigarette habit through her associa.
ton with Keefer, and that, although
serving wines on her table, she was
never intoxicated until her husband
brought home some cocktails that
were drugged.


Mrs. Keefer's charges that her hus-
band swore at her and at her daugh-
ter, Elinor Macy, were upheld by the
statement of her son when he took
the stand. Jack Macy told of the
fight with his stepfather at a local
club because Keefer cursed his sis
ter.

tically supported Keefer and her chill
dren since 1906, from the estate of her
first husband. She said that now her
holdings amount to only about Sly $40
Her suit was for $4,000 a year per-
manent alimony.


Judge Bell, however, held that she
was entitled to neither alimony nor
attorneys fees, and adjudged that
she should pay the costs of litigation

NEW YORK. Oct. 1O.-The coffee
market has again continued to advance
this week and prices have reached new
high levels for the season. European
and Brazilian interests have been very
large buyers and cables from these
sources indicate a very bullish feeling
even at this level There has been con-
siderable liquidation and ofit-taking
with only slight reactions when offer
ings became heavy. However, many
consider the technical situation consid-
erably weakened by the transfer of very
large quantities OF options from strong
interests into the hands of scattered
and probably weaker holders


Stocks of coffee at Rio and Santos are
now about 3.250,00 bags. an increase Of
nearly 100000 bags since the begin
ming Of the season.


More cables Of very bullish nature
were received this week some reducing
estimates of the next Santos crop to
100000 bags. This is very much less
than has heretofore been expected, and
many traders argue against such a large
reduction from previous estimates at
this time of the year. as recent cables
have failed to show any very unfavor-
able weather conditions in Brazil.

The navy yard men have five more

dren of the camp. Last Monday week
was the first. Last year the employees
met the expenses of the camp for one
week and entertained the little ones.
This year they decided that they could
entertain more children by dividing the
time over seven weeks. taking Monday
of each week.


B. p Donnelly, chief gunner of the
Washington navy yard, is chairman OF
the outing committee and all of the
children seem to know it. He is all over

JOHANNESBURG. South Africa, July
5.-Bloody riots connected with the
general strike of the gold miners on
the Rand. which caused the death OF
four civilians and the wounding Of
fifty others in a fight yesterday be-
tween the strikers and the troops, con-
tinued throughout the night.


At midnight mob looted a gun
smiths store and firing became gen.
eral. Squads of cavalry with drawn
swords patrolled all the streets, fire.
quently charging and scattering groups
of rioters, who constantly collected
again to loot the stores and to de-
stroy the electric lamps, the light from
which helped the troops to discover
the disturbers' whereabouts.


Firing was incessant for hours after
midnight in the riot area and many
further casualties occurred, but it was
impossible to obtain accurate details.

Constant dripping will wear away a

Slowly but none the less surely Evelyn
began to let go. To retain her own dig

ling intellect and vivid personality, she
could not easily assume the role of on
locker, but the lesson was at length
learned, the impossible accomplished, and

When the young people voiced their

when Barbara denounced suffragettes
and Betty with equal ardor defended them
when John misquoted her favorite au-
thor, and Phil labeled the brightest mod
ern essayist as "beastIy commonplace,

stander.


1t was not that they did not care for

but as a maiden aunt and not as a COM
panion. 1t never occurred to them that
individually she had no existence-that
under their deadly egotism her mind was

ground to pieces.


Oddly enough her brother-in-law. lazy,
selfish Tom Reade, understood her better
than all the others. And upon one occa-

-1HEN Evelyn Doane's parents died

whelming that her sisters suggestion to

her was accepted gratefully. To be alone
was more than Evelyn could endure. and

household to help her bear her bereave-
ment.


In a surprisingly short time everything
was arranged, and it was not until she
had looked her last upon her familiar old
home that the first doub: as to the wis
dom of her accession assailed her.


But Mrs Reade was SO thoughtful, the
Young people so affectionate, that her
fears soon vanished, and from a strictly
material standpoint she was certainly
well placed. Everything was done for
her comfort. and during the early months
of her bereavement, nothing else mat
tered.


At the end of her second year, however,
when her nerves had regained their tone
and she began to feel an interest in living
once more, she made the startling dis
covery that during her deep mourning
the family had by unanimous consent laid
her gently but firmly upon the shelf

ary change. for the present Engineer

n rule, his municipal creed and policy

DENVER, COLO, Jan. 16.--The en-
tire Pacific coast was practically cut off
from communication with the East to-
day. Heavy rains and SHOWS. together
with wind storms, paralyzed wire COM
munication and caused slides and
blockades that crippled all traffic.
Wires west of Denver on all routes
were lost shortly after midnight. The
storms have been raging in the noun
tains and have been particularly heavy
on the western slope. The storm eX-
tends practically from San Diego to
Seattle and wires along the coast are
said to be out of commission.


Trans continental trains on all lines
are seriously delayed, according to re-
ports received here.


East of Denver heavy fogs prevail
and wires are working poorly. North
ern, centra! and southern routes west
are all affected by the storm and the
tie-up is one of the most complete in
recent years. Throughout the central
west mild, rainy weather is reported.

PEkING, January g. 1913.


A prncely parsonage who has just re-
turned from the Forbidden city says
that the immense precincts of the winter
palace are absolutely deserted save for
the empress dowager and the child en-
peror and a few hundred eunuchs. All
the princesses, all the occupants of the
the imperial clan have silently disap-
peared, leaving the empress and her child
alone.


The same hundreds Of sheep, pigs and
fowls stipulated by the imperial house
hold ordinances are still daily slaughtered.
but, being uneaten. are sold outside. The
eunuchs left uncontrolled, are rapidly
stripping the palaces of their valuables.
The empress dOwager weeps ceaseless-
ly. but dare not proceed to the summer
palace, since Manchu gossips have cruelty
warned her that she will be butchered
the instant she is caught outside the city.
The emperor is dull, listless child, not
knowing what has happened. He plays
ceaselessly with toy soldiers in the halls
and tagged courtyards that were trodden
by the feet not only of his illustrious an
cestors, but by Kubbai Khan himself, and
which once rang to the hurrahs of horse
men returning from the conquest of half
Asia.


Another Rostand would be required to
immortalize this Chinese Aiglon, who is
destined to live and perish miserably as
his prototype, but 1t is signal disgrace
that the palace and it's treasures are not
carefully guarded and converted into
museums, such as the Moscow Kremlin,
thus leaving to the nation some record
of it's departed glory.

to a little four year-old waif who was
placed in her room at police headuuar-

again.


A remarkable resemblance Of the lit
tie Harper girl to the lost daughter

reversed the decision of the commerce
court declaring void the order of the
interstate commerce commission, is

railway, reducing rates from New Or

the long and short haul clause of the
Hepburn law was intended to correct.

charged rate from New Orleans to

raised.

terminating whether or not the higher
rate was reasonable and issued an in

ically into a destroying atmospheric
demon which sweeps over the country
with terrific force until, its energy
spent, the clouds loose their water upon
the earth.

the surcharged clouds lowered above

hamlets below

Remorseless. dry-eyed. deserted by

ed upon with horror by the people Of

forced her young daughter to aid her
in drowning her two stepchildren at

ecutor, and states that he will do
everything in his power to send his

Hated Husbands Children.


The crime was committed Wednes-

fessed Thursday Possessed of deep
