gled them and held them under the
water until both were dead.

discovered by the father He imme-
diately accused his wife, and a Coro-
ner's Jury was summoned. She was
held for first degree murder ana her
daughter as an accessory. That night,

eral, a mob gathered and went to the
county Jail. Sheriff Finch had been

| dren had been the bane Of her exist
ence. She said that she came upon

| gan to call her vile names. and she

drown them.

Let's drown them, Floy," the moth
er is alleged to have said. The girl at

clares that when her mother choked

text:
Spring had come back to Leadam
Street The moist cobblestones had
steamed in the new sun all the after
noon; sparrows were sweeping up to the
caves, trailing strings and long straws
after them; from the back porches OF
the fats were loud. awaking. tinny
sounds. breaking the long silence. The
clank OF the cable cars was borne over
the roofs, clearly now in the damp,
heavy atmosphere; from somewhere
came the Jingle of street piano. Float
ing down the mild afternoon came the
deep, mellow note of some big propeller,
loosing her winter moorings at last and
rousing to greet the tug that would tow
her out of the narrow river. Kelley, the
policeman, strolled along the sidewalk.
with his hands locked behind him, his
nose in the air, smiling eagerly and
pleasurably. He had left of his skirted
overcoat, and changed his clumsy cap
for his helmet.


Annie had sat at her window all the
afternoon, but, as the spring day wore
toward its close, she began to realize
that only the melancholy, and none or
the promise OF this first spring day had
touched her. She had thrown open the
window, to test the quality OF the air.
Now and then a warm breath came wan
dering in of the prairies, though when
II met the cold persistent wind from the
lake 1t hesitated. and timidly turned
back. But Annie would not let herself
doubt that the spring had come. She
knew that in time the prairie wind would
WOO its way until It would be playing
with the waves Of the lake itself, the
little waves that danced all day. blue
and white, in the sunshine. And then
the summer would come, and on Sun
day afternoons Jimmy would take her
out to Lincoln Park and they would
have their supper at Fishers Garden.


Ieadam Street was dull enough on
week days: on Sundays it was wholly
mournfu!.


Once Annie saw a woman. with a
shawl over her head and a tin bucket
in her hand, go into Englehardt's place,
down the street. The woman went In
furtively. and brushed hastily through
the Family Entrance" though why
could not be told. She went there nearly
every hour of the day. Then Annie was
left alone. She did not turn inward to
the nat; that was too still and lonesome.
and II was growing dark now. as the
shadows gathered. She heard the siren
uous gongs of the cable cars over in
State Street. and she could imagine the
crowds. gay from their Sunday holiday,
that filled them, Clinging even to the
running-b boards. She might have gone
out and been with them, as every one
else in the street seemed to have done,
but she would not for worlds have been
away from home when Jimmy came.
She heard the Jingle Of the street piano.
too: she wished it would come down that
way She would gladly have emptied
her purse for the dagO.


1t was not unusual for Annie to be
left alone, and she had grown used to
it-almost: as used a woman can
even the wife of a politician. Jimmy had
told her that she must not worry at any
OF his absences; an alderman could never
tell what might detain him. She had but
a vague notion of the things that might
detain an alderman. though she had no
doubt of their importance. At times she
thought she felt an intimate little charm
in the importance that thus reflected it.
self upon her. but. nevertheless, her heart
was never quite easy until she heard
Jimmys step on the stair and his key
in the latch. and then-jOy came to the
little fiat. and stayed there. trembling
and fearful. until he he went awav again.
She had grown TO be so dependent on
Jimmy. Ever since she had been grad
uated from the convent his great. strong
personality had stood between her and
the world. so that. as her girlhood had
merged into womanhoOd. she had hardly
recognized the change. and she remained
a girl still alone but for him: he was
her whole life She had doubted MS en-
trance into politics at first, just as she
had doubted his going into the saloon
business. though she scarcely understood
either in their various significances.
Father DauEherty mad told her she was
a fortunate girl to have Jimmy for
husband. and that had been enough. Her
only objection was that politics seemed
TO keep Jimmy away from home oftener
than the old work in the packing house
used to; she had trembled at it at times.
and at times had grown a little fright
ened. His success in politics had pleased
her of course, and made her proud, but
il could not have made her prouder Of
him than she had been. He was all
sufficient for her; no change could make
any difference. Without Jimmy,
what could she have done? He had never
been gone so long before: here it was
Sunday evening; he had left at II o'clock
Saturday morning; there was to be an
extra session of the council Saturday
night an unusual thing, and she had
not been surprised when she awoke to
find that it was Sunday morning-and
that Jimmy had not come.


The morning wore away. and she had
made all the arrangements for the din
had gone about lightly. happily, all the
day. singing to herself. the gladness of
the new spring in her. But, one by one,
all the tasks she could think of were per-
formed, even TO drawing the water for
his bath and laying out his clean linen.

NEW ORLEANS, Sept. 27.-Cotton
was climbing to new altitude records
to-day until just at the close, when
a rumor, entirely uncorroborated, came
from Washington to the effect that
Oscar Underwood had introduced a
radical bill aimed against futures
trading.


On this rumor the ring went crazy.
Pandemonium broke loose and every
man tried to sell his neighbor. There
was no support and in the few min
utes before the gong October broke
from 1898 to 1854 The other active
months followed.


New York had just closed for the
week when the news came. The panic
reigned only for the few minutes be-
fore the New Orleans gong.


According to the rumor, Under
woods bill is more radical than any
thing Senator Clarke proposed, and
Clarke's bill would have wiped out the
cotton Exchange.

the usual jeers from the rowdy ele-
ment

and the mixers covered the eight miles
to Elk Ridge, Md, where the luncheon
stop was made, In excellent time.

Training is under way under an en-

Blossom has inaugurated the system of
dividing the candidates into a varsity
squad OF thirty players and of gathering
all the other candidates into class mines,

sity player-Bernie Tommers, pitcher for

players show class they will be pushed

made almost continuously.


Several new baseball diamonds will be
ready for the class teams this spring
and regular series of games will be
played for the class championship.


Yale officials expect to find that the
new baseball cage will improve the team
about % per cent. Yale has had no
cage for three or four years, and all
the indoor work that has been possible
has been some passing and pitching on
the gymnasium floor. No indoor batting
has been allowed, and actual fielding
has been, Of course, impossible. On the
tightly packed dirt floor of the new cage
regular diamond has been laid out,
and several lanes for pitching practice
and for batting have been built Regular
infield work will be possible all win
ter for the first time at Yale.

ordinarily cast down a baseball captain.
but Blossom is not disheartened by the

ems. the freshmen pitchers of last wear.

ever before, as the Easter recess will
begin March 1s, and the team has games

DENVER, July 19.-Mrs. Whitney
Newton, a Denver society matron, has
new pet.


Young Robert Newton came home a
few evenings ago and brought a baby
pig with him


Mrs. Newton took the squirming
animal into her arms and tried to
make it comfortable, but without sue
cess. Finally, in desperation, she
went to the linen closet, took out a
fine piece Of hemstitched linen, en-
broidered with blue flowers, wrapped
it gently about the slick little pig,
then laid him cautiously upon the
downy pillows beside her own.


Piggy gave a satisfied little squeak,
doubled up his feet and went off TO
sleep happily.


This cunning act won Mrs. New
tons heart, and from evaporation
she developed a positive liking for
her pet. His white skin is washed,
combed and perfumed and he sleeps
in downy bed every night beside mis-
mistress. He also eats from a silver
spoon.

Special Cable 70 The Washington Herald.


Berlin, Nov. 1.-The mad King Otto of
Bavaria has been seen by one other'than
the doctors who attend him in the lonely
castle of Furstenried near Munich. An
artist, who happened to stray TO the
castle grounds where a Broken wall was
being repaired caught glimpse OF the
King with physician


THE King walked toward me-" writes
the unwelcome visitor. then remained
standing staring steadfastly, into the
depths of the forest. His features were
sharply cut, his colorless eyes were half
concealed under his bushy eyebrows; his
disheaveled hair is turning fast from
blond to gray. He wore dark suit; his
right hand played restfessly with his
walking stick. His thin, lips occasionally
parted with a twitching movement"


The astonishing thing Is that the King
does not at all look like a madman. but
makes the impression Of one lonely, tired,
embittered.


After gazing intently into the nearby
forest for while he turned suddenly and
walked of with long, rapid steps, cutting
of the heads of flowers with his cane"

London, Nov 1.-The English take their
lSiancing more seriously than any nation.
Now the question arises, '1s not London
tango mad?" Always a foe to innova-
tions. London has held OF from the new
dances, as witness the battles waged on
account of the one-step and Argentine
glide"


Against the new complicated tango are
all the young dancing men. who are too
languid to apply themselves to learn the
seventy two steps needful. On the other
hand, not only the girls, but married
women are throwing gold pieces after
dancing masters and developing great
proficiency. At most country houses tango
teachers are brought from London. but
still the men hold back mutterings.
Jolly rot I call It"

parties.


One thing is certain-the tango will nev-
er penetrate the typical ball room of
England for the reason of lack of space.

waltzes and two-steps will be tolerated.

confessed murder of the children of
James Yates, caused county officials
to-day to place a special guard about

expected tonight.


Mrs Yates, second wife OF James

that she had drowned the two chill
dren of Yates first wife. Her daugh-

ris, was with her, and, according to
the story, aided in the crime.


The killing occurred Wednesday.
Mrs. Yates found the two children. a
boy, IL, and his sister, 10, swimming
in creek that ran through the
Yates farm. She ordered them to
leave the water. The boy, she said,
called her vile names. She became
enraged at him, she said, and, seiz-
ing him by the throat, held his head
under the water until he drowned.


The lads sister screamed and tried
to escape, but was caught by the Far
ris girl, the woman said, and was
drowned as her brother had been.


The children's bodies were found in
the creek Wednesday night. Yester-
day Mrs. Yates and her daughter were
arrested. The woman confessed to-
day.


Her husband to-day declared he
would use every effort to see that his
wife was hanged for the crime.

The shortage of several popular
lines Of wash fabrics for the current
summer season has brought out a
much stronger demand for colorei
dress linens and ramies. Colored
ratines, which did not sell well earlier
in the season. are also good property
at the present time. Several promi-
nent importers in the linen trade
predict that before the month is over
there will be a shortage of cOlored
dress linens, and that within the next
80 days buyers will find stocks COM
pletely exhausted.


Summer weather of the real soft
has brought out an Unexpectedly
large share of the business. The
setback suffered earlier in the season
through the remarkable popularity
of ratines is being rapidly overcome.


Importers are not doing very much
at the present time in the way of
new business except in a few cases
where goods are available for spot
or early delivery.


Stock lots of colored linens ana
linen ramies have been sought for,
and have found a ready market.
Goods on fall order are being charged
up as delivery dates fall due, and
in a good many cases shipments sent
out WouIu De CONSIDERABLY heavier II
the goods were available. Shipments
from abroad are not prompt. and
importing houses are forced to wait
until goods arrive even where they
are past due on old contracts.


Women who buy dress linens know
that these goods have now become
an all-the year-around article, and
the linen gown made up for sum
mer wear gives excellent satisfac-
ton as a house dress during the cool
months. Advices from abroad state
that buyers are hesitating over pay
ing prices current for forward con-
tracts, and are not placing many con-
tracts at present. Yarns hold strong
and the chances of seeing lower
prices on the finished goods in the
near future is very remote.


Mail advices from Belfast state
that the market has been quiet but
steady, and there has been little in
the way of quotable change compared
with previous weeks. Buyers hest
tate to pay the prices current for
forward contracts, and consequently
are only operating in a hand-to-
mouth fashion, as necessity compels
them. There is, however, a hopeful
feeling.

MIDDLEBORO, Mass, August 2-The
battle of Middleboro, which was fought
today. ended the week Of mimic warfare
Of Connecticut. Rhode Island and Massa-
chusetts militiamen in the southeastern
part Of the state.


For more than two hours the red and
blue armies Unanswered and much gun
powder was burned. The war correspond
ents declared the battle drawn. Before
making a decision the army umpires will
study for some weeks the working out of


the problems by the two commanders.
The invading red army's campaign was
to capture Middleboro and get between


the blue army and its base Of supplies.
forty miles away at Framingham. The
problem of the defending blue was to
unite its two wings and hold the town.
When fighting stopped both armies were
in Middleboro with the blues on one side
of the railroad station firing at the reds
on the other side Of the. tracks.
The troops left for home this after
noon.

The Dixie hospital is the only pub

and the new building and equipment
equal If they do not surpass those of
any other hospital in the state. The
institution was founded in 1891 by
Miss Alice NJ. Bacon and during the
twenty-five years of its history has
cared for nearly 4,3OO patients. while
1873 colored nurses have taken courses
in the training school.


Its present situation is an excellent
one, being on the trolley line between
Old Point Comfort and Hampton. the
site of the former residence of Presi-
dent Tyler, near the Hampton bridge,
the grounds extending from the street
back to Hampton creek. The substan-
tial brick building. standing well back
from the street and shaded by fine
trees, is in the form of double cross
ment. Its total length from front to
back is 16S feet and its total width
about 100 feet

ed from the hospital by a solid brick
wall above the kitchen floor, is the
nurses home and will accommodate
forty nurses. twenty-five being at pres
ent in residence. Sitting and sewing
rooms, shady piazza and separate
dining and serving rooms help to make
the home most comfortable and pleas
ant

southern exposure. sunny piazzas and
rooms looking over the water, is most
attractive On the first floor are wards.
private rooms and diet kitchens for
colored patients and on the second
floor the same provision for white pa
tients. Besides the four wards on
these floors. there are two overflow
wards in the third story and fourteen
private rooms in all. The construction
is of the latest type advised for hos
pitals. with no panels In the doors and
no corners I'm the rooms, dark window
shades, moving both up and down. and
the very best sanitary equipment in
toilets and bathrooms.


The operating and sterilizing rooms,
situated in the center of the building
and near the elevator from the receiv-
ing room, into which the ambulance
entrance opens, are provided with the
most up to date appliances possible to
obtain. Besides the rooms mentioned.
there are the necessary administrative
offices and rooms for the doctors and
hospital STAFF. Sixty patients can easi-
ly be accommodated.

A sudden rise of temperature in

velops a low pressure area, into the

every point Of the compass. If there is
sufficient difference in the temperature
of this locality and the surrounding
districts, the swirl of winds grows mag
ically into destroying atmospheric
demon which sweeps over the country

spent. the clouds loose their water upon
the earth.

in Omaha and brought death and de-
struction to the city, later travelling
eastward and causing the nations
greatest tragedy, had its beginning in
the state of Washington about March
It, according to VonHerrmann. The
cyclonic conditions were developed in
the manner described, and moved
swiftly eastward over the Western
states, demolshing homes, public
buildings and farm houses as they
went.


When the middle West was reached,
the force was greatly spent, and just as
the surcharged clouds lowered above
the river valleys of Ohio and Indiana,
they burst and deluged the cities and
hamletS below

days was one of the fastest sailing craft
in service on the Chesapeake. About
sixteen years ago she was purchased by
Capt. Theodore Ballenger of Alexandria,
who had her rebuilt and made practical
ly a new vessel, and gave her the name
she now bears. She was used In the
fish and oyster running industry and
about six years ago was purchased by
Capt. Neitzy and Capt. Faunce and
placed in fishing service on the river. She

feet deep, and will carry about twenty
five tons. Alexandria is her hailing port.

Conrad Won Hoetzendorf is famous IN
Austria as friend and creature of the
militant Archduke Franz Ferdinand. This
fame bellies him. He would have come
to the top under any conditions But the
archduke discovered him. Before the
archduke made the discovery Conrad had
merely a local fame with his regiment,
with his brigade, with his division. He
was born fifty years ago as son or a
good soldier, and he rose by his own
talents to be commander OF the eighth
infantry division. which is stationed at
Innsbruck.


The eighth division worshiped him, and
showed its worship in the nickname der
liebenswuerdige Schinder'-the kindly
hangman-a nickname which admirapiy

yond that people knew only that the
brilliant general had written three books
upon tactics, and that these books main
ly reiterated the good counsel to army
officers not to read books about TACTICS
but to prepare to fight battles


Franz Ferdinand discovered Conrad
during the south Tyrol maneuvers. These
maneuvers are held with the invariable
aim of testing the south Tyrol defenses
against an Italian raid. The almost UNI
known Hoetzendorf here developed the
relentless energy and daring leadership
of a Napoleon. He sent his battalions
to scale precipices which the wisest guide
books declared unscalable; drove them
over "impracticable passes, and got
them to turn UP everywhere except where,
they were expected. The exhausted sol>
diers swore at their hard lot but worked
like blacks for their adored kindly
hangman.' and the kindly .hangman."
who worked and swore harder than any
one. kissed his officers and men in joy
at their achievements. In those days gem
tlemanly old Baron Won Beck was chief
of staff. He was Mortified at seeing war
made in this original way. and he did not
conceal his displeasure with the lightning
Conrad.


After the maneuvers Archduke Franz
Ferdinand interviewed. He had witnessed
Conrad's terrific way of practicng for
war, and witnessed also Beck's horror.
He got rid Of Beck. though IT cost sew
eral angry interviews at Schoenbrunn be-
fore the aged kaiser consented.

From the St Louis Republic


An underground concert was one Of the
features of the convention of the Mis-
souri, Music Teachers Association at
Joplin the last week. A band of intrepid
musicians donned slickers. clambered
into the tub. and were whitfield down
through the Stygian shaft to the soo-foot
level. They were . bit distract when
they de-tubbed, so to speak. They doubt
less repented the rash impulse which
moved them to leave far. far behind the
smiling green landscape and the glorious
sunshine and the happy. singing birds
which make up the paradise known as
earths surface. But the Rubicon had


been crossed, or, rather. plumbed. and
here they were in the nav of a Joplin
zinc mine. and it was theirs to feign
valor they did not possess.


But after cropping along through an
endless tunnel for perhaps two or three
eternal minutes they came to a vaulted
chamber. which made them rub their
eyes in wonder. 1t was high and vast.
and ablaze with electric bulbs that
popped profusely forth from walls and
roof. They saw panels of zinc ore rum


ming a riot of color from pale topaz TO
the red of the rubys heart-an iridescent
sheen. They saw lead glittering in the


rocky sides They saw great ribs OF
flint. hard and white and taut under
the weight of the burden which once bent
the shoulders Of Atlas They saw chaste


strips of tiff woven into a marvellous


geologic frieze, and with the imagination


of musicians they wondered. perhaps, If


the ceaseless drip of the water were the
grief of this stone because the world


had not accounted it precious. They
saw stalactites pink and purple and


softly yellow as Etruscan gold. And they


saw the man who fashions those strange
ornate caverns and who. like the work


he does. is mostly unknown. and, alto
gether unsung, artisan and artist, the
Joplin zinc miner, who in the emergencies
always essays 100 per cent pure stun
Then the musicians sang. and they


sang in the most beautiful mine in the
world-a Missouri zinc mine.

One feature of the parcel post on which
t seems emphasis has not been laid is
that Ii is another step toward blotting
out rural isolation. 1t is one more means
of bringing the countryman into closer
contact with the city man and with city
ways. A tendency has been very strongly
this way for quarter of a century, and
its results have been so obvious that the
countryman with wisp of hay in his
hair and straw in his mouth is rarely
seen outside old homestead plays and
comic supplements


the steam railroad penetrated into
country districts and the electric car
has brought vast farm area into touch
with the city. A few minutes ride brings
man from pastoral to metropolitan
scenes. and from quiet rural lanes into
busy. throbbing streets. 1t also takes
city man quickly from the great areas of
asphalt. artificial stone and brick to green
turf. yellow clay and sandy stretches.
The .evening-up process goes an at both
ends


The telephone brings city and country
within speaking distance of each other.
and telephone wires strung along roads.
through woods and over fields and mead
ows have done much to take from the
country that dull isolation which was
such a frequent complaint against coun-
try life. Operating to this end with the
telephone has been rural free delivery.


Here is an agency that has carried the
daily newspaper into farmhOuses and
whetted and encouraged the reading habit,
prompting people already back on the
land to keep step in the procession of
the times.


In connection with all these agencies of
rural Improvement have come automobiles
and the demand for better roads. and
finally an awakening of everybody in
city and country to the manifold and
mutual advantages of good roads.


And now the parcel post furnishes an
other connecting link between town and
country.

TERRE HAUTE. Ind, March 2b.--
Charity and human brotherhood were
being severely tried In this city today,
SO hours after tornado killed 20 per.
sons, injured over 200 and wiped out
all trace Of Ave other persons.

mittees have engaged to feed. clothe
and re-start in life nearly three hun
dred dispossessed working men and
their families. Mayor Gerhardt was
compelled to issue q threat to punish
any storekeeper found charging ex-
orbitant prices fofr food.


The authorities and the inhabitants
of Terre Haute only today awoke
from the daze that followed the
disaster Three public schools housed
the homeless and there they were fed
also.

promised help toward a new start In
life. Furniture will be bought with
public funds and will be presented to
families who cannot otherwise replace
their ruined belongings. The tornado
wiped out O working class section

the well-to-do were wrecked. Scores
of the homeless have found refuge
with relatives and friends.

with the small donations of the work
ing classes rather than with the big
pledges Of the rich. Not quite $4,000
had been subscribed this morning.


State troops patrolled the wrecked
area. Work OF searching the debris
for more bodies went forward slowly.
Practically nothing has been done to
reclaim the district laid waste.

Traffic communication with the flood
stricken sections OF the Middle and
Southwest continues uncertain. Some
improvement, however. in schedule time
between Washington and Chicago has
been made. Oficisls at the Union Sta
ton state that trains over the Pennsyl-
vania and Baltimore and Ohio are max
ing the run with six and eight hours
delay. In comparison with the ten 10
twenty hours delay Friday. this is a de-
cided improvement.


The rapidly rising waters Of the Ohio
River complexities the problem of keep
ing the Western lines open. Flood
waters in the Ohio River effectually have
cut of communication with Cincinnati
and Louisville over the Chesapeake and
Ohio Railway. This line was heavily
used until yesterday for the rushing of
supplies and passengers to adjacent
points in the flooded territory.


officers at Union Station said last
night that tickets were being sold only
10 Huntington. W. Va. over the Chesa-
peake and Ohio. and that the train dis
pstchers are uninformed how serious a
blow the rise OF the Ohio River will
strike at the Southern Railway traffic.
Many passengers for points further West
are being held in Huntington today, un-
certain to when conditions may per-
nit their taking up their journey. Rail-





the lines open. and are fighting every
foot of further encroachment of the
floods


Northern Route Used.


While schedules have improved some
what between here and Chicago, trains
over both the Pennsylvania and the
Baltimore and Ohio are forced to keep
10 the northern route. They go from
Pittsburg by way of Alliance, Cleveland.
and thence TO Chicago over the tracks
of the Lake Shore and Michigan South
ern.


Connections with most of the flooded
cities in Southern Ohio and Indiana have
not been resumed. The trunk line of the
Pennsylvania line to st. Louis, known
as the Panhandle. is still impossible.
All connections with this territory are be-
ing made by way of Chicago.


Supplies and mails are being regularly
forwarded from Washington, but the Of
ficials have no idea when they will be
delivered.


With communication with Cincinnati
over the Chesapeake and Ohio cut off
by the Ohio, the di1>ulties in the way
of getting supplies and medical relief to
the stricken towns is increased. Reports
received by the railroad officials in Wash
ington furnish little encouragement, but
all supplies are being forwarded as soon
as received. and every effort is being
made TO deliver them.

The big Hamburg-American liner
Amerika, outward bound. ran aground to-
day off Tompkinsville, Staten Island, and
Immediately hoisted the Signal Not I'M
der control


The Amerika left her pier few min
utes after o'clock this morning and
began nosing her way down the harbor
in sixty-mile gale. Owing to last night 8
violent wind and it's continuation today
the tide was very low-nearly three feet
below normal-and because of this the big
vessel stuck in the mud. Sheltered as
she was in the lee of Staten Island and
the Brooklyn shore, her condition was not
serious, and her commander hoped to
float her with the rising tide late today.


Most Severe Storm in Years.


Belated returns of the damage done by
the storm of yesterday and last night,
reaching the telegraph companies here to-
day, revealed that clean sweep of the
wires had been made from Jacksonville to
Maine and that the storm was the most
severe of recent years. Thousands of
men are at work today repairing the dam
age.


Perhaps the greatest damage to wires
was done at East Buffalo, where the tail
of the storm leveled telegraph poles for a
mile. A sixty-mile gale ragged there stimuli
taneously with the passage OF the main
storm off to sea from the New England
coast.


Washington Wires Broken.


High winds prevailed today along the
northern Atlantic seaboard, but the wire
trouble. it was reported, was slight COM
pared with that of yesterday. The most
serious instance today was the break
near Philadelphia of more than sixty
through wires between New York and
Washington.


Daybreak today found the coast from
Florida to Maine dotted with camps OF
linemen, many of whom had worked all
night in the darkness.

private system telephones at the gar

switchboard was taken out The tele-

fusing to use the others switchboard

which are not Bell telephones. are

Henry Johnson, colored, fifty years old,
who was employed in the bureau of en-
craving and printing, committed suicide
in the bathroom at his home, 2459 p
street northwest, this morning by cutting
his throat.


Joseph Johnson, ten-year-old son Of the
dead man, returned home from school
about 1890 o'clock and was unable to
get the bathroom door open. He could
not find his father, the housekeeper was
away and his sisters were at their places
of employment.


The boy summoned Martha and Clara
Sewell from the adjoining house and told
them of his troubles. They soon had
the bathroom door open and found the
dead body Of Johnson with his head rest
ing on the edge Of the tub, the razor
which he had used being still grasped
in his hand


Life had been extinct several hours. 1t
is thought that Johnson killed himself
shortly after the boy went to school. The
police were unable to learn any reason
for the deed.

Visitors to Washington are often

Some of the most interesting among

Dixons five little girls. The Swager

The little Baroness Hengelmuller,

army, a complimentary title purely,

vastly more envied than the boys who
merely have Rough Rider suits or
Boy Scout uniforms. The three chill
dren are being given every advantage

BRIDGETON, n. J.. August 30.--After
mourning four years for her last born
baby. who she believed had been buried
in infancy, Mrs. Beatrice Gaddis. a young
widow of this city, has learned that the
child is living with a well-to-do Phila-
dephia family.


In 1909. when Mrs. Gaddis was living
in Mauch Chunk, Pa. her husband was
killed in coal mine explosion. Soon
after that she became a mother in
Mauch Chunk hospital. There was an
other mother in the hospital. and this
woman's child died. The nurse in charge
of the two cases realized that Mrs. Cad
dis was a poor widow with four other
children, whereas the other woman was
of a family that had much money. The
nurse exchanged the babies, giving Mrs.
Gaddis the other mothers dead child,
and giving Mrs. Gaddis' living baby to
her ward companion.


A few days ago Mrs. Gaddis received
word from the nurse, still in Maunch
Chunk, to come there instantly. She
went and found the nurse upon her
deathbed. There was also the other
woman. The nurse told the story and
for the first time the two mothers knew
the truth. The nurse begged forgive
ness before she died. and this was grant
ed by the women.


Then the woman who had possession
of the Gaddis child appealed to Mrs.
Gadds for the custody of the little girl
who had been brought up as her own.
She pointed out that Mrs. Gaddis never
had known her daughter and had four
other children. whereas the little one
was the only child the Philadelphia home
ever had known.


Mrs. Gaddis yielded to the entreaues
and has taken legal, steps to permit her
child to be adopted into the home which
she supposes is hers by birthright.

infant mortality being waged by the
Atlanta Mothers Congress is making
great progress, but more contribu-
lions must be had if the hundreds Of
needy babies in the city are to be
supplied with the free milk which is
most necessary Statistics show that
infant mortality is greatest during
the heated months of July, August
and September.


Atlanta has generous people who
can spare the small amount which
would mean life and health to baby,
which, without proper nourishment,
is fighting a hopeless fight against
disease and death. Many have con-
tributed, but more money is urgently
needed, and every days delay in
turning in your contribution means
that much less chance of life being
saved.


The Mothers Congress has already
distributed milk tickets to number
of needy mothers, but there are many
more who can not buy milk necessary
to nourish their babies.

ing from lack of the food that few

1856 Pine Street, will gladly take care
of your contribution for you.

likely culminate in an organized rebel
lion.


This crisis in many respects resembles
that which beset the United States at the
time of the civil war.


In Natal, the largest province of United
South Africa, the situation is gravest

employers expected that when the con-
tracts had expired the Indians would
leave the colony and return to India
